description: Crash Course compares Uranus and Neptune, covering their compositions, unusual magnetic fields and the mysteries of their formation at the edge of the solar system.
takeaway: Uranus and Neptune are ice giants with compositions and magnetic fields that differ markedly from Jupiter and Saturn.

title: Fundamentals of HVAC - Basics of HVAC
coreQuestion: What are the basic principles behind heating, ventilation and air conditioning?
description: Introduces the refrigeration cycle, heat transfer and air distribution that underpin HVAC systems. It gives a broad overview of climate control engineering.
takeaway: HVAC systems move heat using a refrigeration cycle and distribute conditioned air through ducts.

title: Copycats! This Ant Is Surrounded By Imposters | Deep Look
coreQuestion: How do impostor ants infiltrate a colony without being detected?
description: Investigates ants that mimic the chemical signatures of another species to live among its workers. It explains recognition chemistry and the evolutionary arms race between host and parasite.
takeaway: Insect societies depend on chemical identity, making scent a battleground for deception.

title: Is this one connected curve, or two? Bet you can't explain why...
coreQuestion: How can you tell whether a single curve is connected or secretly two?
description: Morphocular probes the subtleties of connected curves and why intuition about 'one piece' can mislead.
takeaway: Connectedness is a topological property, not a matter of drawing without lifting the pen.

title: The REAL Three Body Problem in Physics
coreQuestion: Why does adding one more body make the gravitational two-body problem unsolvable in closed form?
description: The two-body problem yields neat ellipses, but three mutually attracting masses defy a general closed-form solution. The video examines the chaos and special periodic orbits that emerge.
takeaway: Three-body gravity is fundamentally chaotic, so long-term prediction requires approximation rather than exact formulas.

title: Jupiter: Crash Course Astronomy #16
coreQuestion: What makes Jupiter the largest planet, and how does it shape the solar system?
description: Crash Course examines Jupiter's immense size, powerful storms and gravitational influence on the rest of the solar system.
takeaway: Jupiter's mass and gravity make it the dominant sculptor of the solar system's architecture.

title: Ceiling fans: the simple idea we keep screwing up
coreQuestion: Why are ceiling fans so often installed and used incorrectly?
description: Examines ceiling fan design, airflow patterns and common installation mistakes that reduce effectiveness. It clarifies what fans actually cool.
takeaway: Ceiling fans cool people, not rooms, and their benefit depends on direction, speed and placement.

title: This Ciliate Is About to Die
coreQuestion: What happens when a ciliate reaches the end of its reproductive lifespan?
description: Journey to the Microcosmos follows a ciliate nearing death, explaining nuclear dimorphism, division limits and the cellular wear that accumulates across generations. It connects microscopic life cycles to ageing biology.
takeaway: Even single-celled organisms face ageing, shaped by how they manage and renew their genetic material.

title: The Subtle Reason Taylor Series Work | Smooth vs. Analytic Functions
coreQuestion: Why do some infinitely smooth functions have Taylor series that fail to represent them?
description: Morphocular explains the gap between smoothness and analyticity, using functions whose Taylor series vanish.
takeaway: Being infinitely differentiable does not guarantee that a Taylor series converges to the function.

title: The Time-Reversibility Paradox - Time Actually Flows Both Ways
coreQuestion: If fundamental physics is time-reversible, why does time seem to flow in only one direction?
description: Microscopic laws run equally well forwards and backwards, yet macroscopic systems show a clear arrow of time. The video unpacks the paradox and the statistical origin of irreversibility.
takeaway: The arrow of time is statistical, not a feature of individual particle laws.

title: The Moon: Crash Course Astronomy #12
coreQuestion: How did the Moon form, and how does it affect Earth?
description: Crash Course explains the leading theory of the Moon's formation from a giant impact and its ongoing effects on Earth's tides and rotation.
takeaway: The Moon is likely the product of a colossal impact and continues to shape Earth's environment.

title: Coffee Percolators: An Explanation and Roast
coreQuestion: How does a coffee percolator repeatedly cycle water through grounds?
description: Explains how heated water rises, percolates through coffee grounds and returns, repeating until brewing is complete. It examines the design's simplicity and limitations.
takeaway: A percolator brews by repeatedly cycling boiling water through grounds, which can over-extract if left too long.

title: Stentors: Single-Celled Giants
coreQuestion: How can a single cell grow large enough to see with the naked eye?
description: Profiles stentors, giant ciliates that can regenerate after being cut and coordinate movement with thousands of cilia. It explores how their large size and nuclear organisation challenge simple ideas about cells.
takeaway: A single cell can achieve surprising size and complexity through specialised internal organisation.

title: How to do two (or more) integrals with just one
coreQuestion: How can a single integral evaluate two different integrals at once?
description: Morphocular demonstrates differentiating under the integral sign to compute multiple integrals from one parameterised integral.
takeaway: Introducing a parameter turns a hard integral into a differential equation you can solve.

title: 3 Physics Paradoxes That Feel Like a Glitch in Reality
coreQuestion: Which everyday-seeming physics puzzles expose genuine tensions in our theories?
description: A set of classic paradoxes, from quantum measurement to relativity, are unpacked to show where intuition fails and where theory itself is incomplete. The discussion links each puzzle to its underlying physical principle.
takeaway: Paradoxes are diagnostic tools that reveal where a physical theory outruns common sense or its own foundations.

title: Most Massive Star in the Universe - Deep Sky Videos
coreQuestion: Which star holds the record for mass, and what makes such stars so unstable?
description: Deep Sky Videos profiles the most massive known star and explains why stars above a certain mass lose material rapidly and live short, violent lives.
takeaway: The most massive stars burn through their fuel quickly and are unstable enough to shed mass in powerful winds.

title: The Antique Microwave Oven that's Better than Yours
coreQuestion: Why might an older microwave oven outperform modern ones?
description: Compares an older microwave's construction and heating behaviour with modern units, questioning what 'better' means. It weighs durability against cost and convenience.
takeaway: Older appliances sometimes prioritise durability and performance over cost and convenience.

title: How Microscopic Hunters Get Their Lunch
coreQuestion: How do microscopic predators capture and consume prey in a crowded microbial world?
description: Shows how tiny hunters use cilia, toxins and engulfment to feed, and how their predation shapes microbial communities. It places these encounters in the broader ecology of ponds and soils.
takeaway: Predation at microscopic scales drives energy flow and diversity in invisible ecosystems.

title: The Surprising Maths of Britain's Oldest* Game Show
coreQuestion: What probability and strategy lurk behind a classic British game show?
description: Another Roof analyses the mathematics behind an old game show, from optimal stopping to scoring strategies.
takeaway: Even entertainment formats encode nontrivial probability and decision problems.

title: MAGNETS: How Do They Work?
coreQuestion: What is actually happening inside a magnet to produce its invisible field?
description: Minutephysics explains magnetism as moving charges and aligned domains, showing how a magnetic field arises and how materials become magnetised. The treatment stays grounded in charge motion rather than mystery.
takeaway: Magnetism is not a separate force but a relativistic effect of moving electric charges.

title: M87 - Infinity in your Hand - Deep Sky Videos
coreQuestion: What makes the galaxy M87 and its central black hole so remarkable?
description: Deep Sky Videos introduces M87, a giant elliptical galaxy whose supermassive black hole was the first ever imaged, along with its powerful jets.
takeaway: M87 hosts a supermassive black hole whose shadow became the first direct image of such an object.

title: Engines haven't been fully mechanical in decades - and that's good!
coreQuestion: Why have engines become increasingly controlled by electronics rather than mechanics?
description: Explains how electronic engine management improved efficiency, emissions and drivability over purely mechanical systems. It shows why mechanical control alone is no longer sufficient.
takeaway: Electronic control lets engines run cleaner and more efficiently than mechanical systems alone could.

title: Hydra: Stretchy, Speedy, & Probably Immortal
coreQuestion: How does Hydra stretch, move and regenerate with such simple tissue organisation?
description: Examines Hydra's flexible body, simple nervous system and remarkable regenerative capacity. It explains how a small cnidarian can rebuild itself and persist for long periods.
takeaway: Simple animals can combine flexible body plans with powerful regeneration to survive repeated damage.

title: What IS a Number? As Explained by a Mathematician
coreQuestion: What is a number, according to a working mathematician?
description: Another Roof asks a mathematician to pin down what 'number' means, moving from counting to formal definitions.
takeaway: A number is less a thing than a role in a structure defined by its operations.

title: General Relativity Explained in 7 Levels of Difficulty
coreQuestion: How does general relativity replace the idea of gravitational force with curved spacetime?
description: Across seven levels of difficulty, the video builds from everyday gravity to Einstein's picture of mass curving spacetime and objects following geodesics. Each level adds precision without losing the core intuition.
takeaway: Gravity is not a pull between masses but the geometry of spacetime telling matter how to move.

title: M11 - Wild Duck Cluster - Deep Sky Videos
coreQuestion: What is the Wild Duck Cluster, and what can it tell us about star clusters?
description: Deep Sky Videos tours the open cluster M11, explaining its age, stellar population and place in the Messier catalogue.
takeaway: Open clusters like M11 are laboratories for studying stars of the same age and composition.

title: Alkaline batteries are obsolete — but not for the reason you'd think
coreQuestion: Why are alkaline batteries considered obsolete despite still being sold everywhere?
description: Explores the chemistry and economics behind alkaline batteries and why newer chemistries have surpassed them. It separates market persistence from technical merit.
takeaway: Alkaline batteries persist for convenience, but their chemistry is outclassed by modern alternatives.

title: The Terrifying Viruses of the Microcosmos
coreQuestion: What roles do viruses play in microbial ecosystems beyond causing disease?
description: Explores viruses that infect microbes, showing how they kill hosts, transfer genes and reshape populations. It reframes viruses as ecological forces, not just pathogens.
takeaway: Viruses are major architects of microbial evolution and nutrient cycling, not merely agents of infection.

title: It Took 2137 Years to Solve This
coreQuestion: Which mathematical problem took over two millennia to resolve, and why?
description: Another Roof tells the story of a classical construction problem and the 2137-year path to its solution.
takeaway: Some ancient problems waited for entirely new branches of mathematics to become solvable.

title: Why E=mc² is wrong
coreQuestion: In what sense is the famous equation E=mc² only a special case?
description: Fermilab clarifies that E=mc² applies to rest energy, while moving particles obey the fuller relation linking energy, momentum and mass. The distinction resolves a common oversimplification.
takeaway: E=mc² is a limiting case; the complete relation accounts for momentum as well as mass.

title: M90 - Jellyfish Galaxy - Deep Sky Videos
coreQuestion: Why does the galaxy M90 appear to trail tentacles of gas and stars?
description: Deep Sky Videos examines M90, a galaxy falling through a cluster and losing gas to ram pressure, producing its jellyfish-like tail.
takeaway: A galaxy moving through hot cluster gas can be stripped of its own gas, triggering star formation in the tail.

title: Old car headlights were all the same — which was a fairly bright idea
coreQuestion: Why did standardising car headlights improve safety and manufacturing?
description: Looks at the history of sealed-beam headlights and the benefits of a common, replaceable design. It shows how standardisation simplified repairs and ensured consistent illumination.
takeaway: Standardising headlights simplified repairs and ensured consistent road illumination.

title: Meet the Microcosmos
coreQuestion: What worlds exist in a single drop of pond water?
description: Introduces the diversity of life visible under a microscope, from ciliates and rotifers to algae and bacteria. It establishes how small-scale observation reveals entire ecosystems.
takeaway: A drop of water contains a complete, interacting community of organisms invisible to the naked eye.

title: The Most Powerful Diagram in Mathematics
coreQuestion: Why is the commutative diagram considered the most powerful diagram in mathematics?
description: Another Roof argues for the commutative diagram as a unifying visual language across mathematics.
takeaway: Commutative diagrams make relationships, not just objects, the primary subject of mathematics.

title: Quantum Gravity
coreQuestion: Why is combining quantum mechanics with general relativity so difficult?
description: Fermilab outlines the clash between the smooth spacetime of relativity and the probabilistic, discrete world of quantum theory, and why a unified description remains elusive. The Planck scale marks where both frameworks must apply.
takeaway: Quantum gravity is needed where spacetime itself becomes subject to quantum uncertainty.

title: Magellanic Clouds (and Apollo 16) - Deep Sky Videos
coreQuestion: What are the Magellanic Clouds, and how do they interact with the Milky Way?
description: Deep Sky Videos explores the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, satellite galaxies of the Milky Way whose gravitational interactions drive star formation.
takeaway: The Magellanic Clouds are nearby dwarf galaxies whose interactions with the Milky Way shape both systems.

title: Air fryers are simpler than you think, but still pretty neat
coreQuestion: What actually makes an air fryer different from a convection oven?
description: Demystifies the air fryer as a compact convection oven with a fast fan and concentrated heat. It explains the cooking physics behind crisp results.
takeaway: An air fryer is essentially a small, fast convection oven, not a new cooking technology.

title: Diatoms: Tiny Factories You Can See From Space
coreQuestion: How do microscopic diatoms influence global oxygen and carbon cycles?
description: Looks at diatoms, their glass-like silica shells and their outsized role in photosynthesis and carbon sequestration. It connects their abundance to planetary-scale climate processes.
takeaway: Microscopic algae with glass shells are major drivers of Earth's oxygen and carbon budgets.

title: When Descartes Challenged Fermat (and Lost)
coreQuestion: How did Fermat beat Descartes in a contest over tangent lines?
description: Another Roof recounts the historical duel between Descartes and Fermat over methods for finding tangents.
takeaway: Fermat's method for tangents anticipated calculus and outperformed Descartes's approach.

title: The Standard Model
coreQuestion: What particles and forces does the Standard Model account for, and what does it leave out?
description: Fermilab surveys the quarks, leptons and gauge bosons that make up the Standard Model, along with its successes and its known gaps such as gravity and dark matter. The result is a concise map of particle physics.
takeaway: The Standard Model is our best description of fundamental particles, but it is deliberately incomplete.

title: M85 - Lenticular Galaxy - Deep Sky Videos
coreQuestion: What is a lenticular galaxy, and how does M85 fit that class?
description: Deep Sky Videos introduces M85, a lenticular galaxy, and explains the features that place it between spiral and elliptical types.
takeaway: Lenticular galaxies like M85 represent a transitional form between spiral and elliptical galaxies.

title: The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): Most Ingenious Algorithm Ever?
coreQuestion: How can the discrete Fourier transform be computed in O(n log n)?
description: Reducible derives the fast Fourier transform by splitting a signal into even and odd samples and exploiting the symmetry of roots of unity. The video shows the recursive structure and butterfly diagram. It explains why the speedup is possible.
takeaway: The FFT's speed comes from reusing intermediate sums that the naive transform recomputes.

title: Film: the reason some of the past was in HD
coreQuestion: Why does some older film footage look sharper than video from decades later?
description: Explains how film's high resolution and video's limitations shaped the apparent quality of historical footage. It compares analog capture media.
takeaway: Film captured far more detail than early video formats, making old footage surprisingly sharp.

title: Paramecium: The White Rat of Ciliates
coreQuestion: Why is Paramecium a model organism for studying cell biology?
description: Explains Paramecium's two nuclei, osmoregulation and genetic behaviour, and why its size and tractability made it a classic experimental subject. It bridges microscopy and cell biology.
takeaway: A common pond ciliate helped establish fundamental ideas about cells, genetics and physiology.

title: Defining Every Number Ever
coreQuestion: How can every number be defined, from 0 to the transfinite?
description: Another Roof surveys the construction of number systems all the way to ordinal and cardinal infinities.
takeaway: Numbers are built in stages, each new layer solving limits the previous one could not.

title: Quantum Field Theory
coreQuestion: How does quantum field theory treat particles as excitations of underlying fields?
description: Fermilab reframes particles as ripples in quantum fields, explaining how interactions arise from field exchange and why this picture underlies the Standard Model. The field viewpoint replaces the older particle-only intuition.
takeaway: In quantum field theory, particles are not objects but quantised excitations of fields that fill space.

title: How James Webb Orbits "Nothing"
coreQuestion: How can a telescope orbit a point in empty space?
description: The James Webb Space Telescope sits near the second Lagrange point, where gravitational and rotational forces balance. Launch Pad Astronomy explains how an orbit around 'nothing' is possible.
takeaway: A Lagrange point is a balance of forces, not a place, and Webb orbits it rather than sitting still.

title: Understanding and Analysing Trusses
coreQuestion: How do trusses distribute loads through triangular members?
description: Introduces truss analysis using joint and section methods to find member forces. It shows why triangular arrangements are structurally efficient.
takeaway: Trusses carry loads through axial forces in members, making their behaviour predictable with simple methods.

title: What is the Evidence for Evolution?
coreQuestion: What observable evidence supports the theory of evolution?
description: Stated Clearly reviews multiple lines of evidence for evolution, including fossils, anatomy, biogeography and DNA. It shows how independent observations converge on common descent.
takeaway: Evolution is supported by converging evidence from fossils, anatomy, geography and genetics.

title: The Ancient Mathematics of the DVD Screensaver
coreQuestion: What mathematics underlies the bouncing DVD logo screensaver?
description: Another Roof analyses the bouncing logo as a billiards problem, explaining when it hits a corner.
takeaway: The screensaver's path is a straight line on an unfolded table, making corner hits a number-theory question.

title: What is Entropy?
coreQuestion: What does entropy actually measure beyond the vague idea of disorder?
description: Entropy is introduced as a count of microscopic arrangements, connecting heat flow, probability and the second law in an accessible way. The explanation replaces the loose 'messiness' metaphor with a precise statistical meaning.
takeaway: Entropy measures how many ways a state can be realised, not merely how messy it looks.

title: The Solar Gravitational Lens will Map Exoplanets. Seriously.
coreQuestion: How could the Sun's gravity be used as a telescope to image exoplanets?
description: The Sun's mass bends light from distant objects, potentially magnifying exoplanets into detailed images. Launch Pad Astronomy explains the physics and the mission concepts behind this idea.
takeaway: The Sun itself could act as a giant lens, turning gravitational bending into an exoplanet imaging tool.

title: 5 Simple Steps for Solving Any Recursive Problem
coreQuestion: How can any recursive problem be broken into a reliable recursive solution?
description: Reducible offers a five-step framework for recursion: identify the base case, shrink the problem, trust the recursion, combine results. The video applies it to classic examples. It clarifies how the call stack carries the work.
takeaway: A correct recursion needs a base case, a smaller subproblem and a way to combine results.

title: The Problem with Stainless Steel
coreQuestion: Why does stainless steel sometimes fail despite its name?
description: Examines corrosion mechanisms in stainless steel, including pitting and stress corrosion cracking. It explains when and why the protective layer breaks down.
takeaway: Stainless steel resists corrosion only when its passive layer remains intact; chlorides can break it down.

title: What is DNA and How Does it Work?
coreQuestion: How does DNA store and transmit biological information?
description: Explains the double helix, complementary base pairing and how DNA replication preserves information across cell divisions. It connects molecular structure to inheritance.
takeaway: DNA's simple paired structure makes accurate copying and inheritance possible.

title: Imaginary Numbers Are Real [Part 1: Introduction]
coreQuestion: Why are imaginary numbers more than a formal trick?
description: Welch Labs begins a series arguing that imaginary numbers have concrete geometric meaning as rotations in the plane.
takeaway: The imaginary unit is a rotation by ninety degrees, not just a symbol for an impossible square root.

title: What Everyone Gets Wrong About E=mc²
coreQuestion: Why is the phrase 'mass converts to energy' a misleading reading of E=mc²?
description: The video untangles common misconceptions, distinguishing rest mass from relativistic mass and explaining when mass is conserved and when energy is. The nuance matters for nuclear and particle physics.
takeaway: Mass and energy are two measures of the same underlying quantity, not substances that turn into one another.

title: Phases and Motions of the Moon
coreQuestion: What causes the Moon's phases, and why does its motion look the way it does?
description: Launch Pad Astronomy explains how the changing angle between Sun, Earth and Moon produces phases, and how the Moon's orbit shapes what we see.
takeaway: The Moon's phases are simply the changing portion of its sunlit face visible from Earth.

title: How Levers, Pulleys and Gears Work
coreQuestion: How do levers, pulleys and gears multiply force or speed?
description: Demonstrates how simple machines trade distance for force using mechanical advantage. It connects basic machines to everyday devices.
takeaway: Simple machines multiply force by increasing the distance over which it is applied.

title: What is Evolution?
coreQuestion: What process produces new species and adapts organisms to their environments?
description: Defines evolution as change in heritable traits over generations and introduces mutation, selection and speciation. It clarifies common misconceptions about progress and purpose.
takeaway: Evolution has no goal; it is the cumulative result of variation, inheritance and selection.

title: The most beautiful equation in math, explained visually [Euler’s Formula]
coreQuestion: How does e raised to i pi equal negative one, and what does that reveal about complex numbers?
description: Welch Labs visualises Euler's formula by connecting the exponential function to rotation on the unit circle, showing why e to the i theta traces cosine and sine. The video builds the identity step by step from complex multiplication and the geometry of the complex plane.
takeaway: Euler's identity is not a coincidence but a natural consequence of defining exponentiation for complex numbers.

title: Quarks Explained in Four Minutes - Physics Girl
coreQuestion: What are quarks, and why can they never be observed alone?
description: Physics Girl introduces the six quark flavours and explains how colour charge and confinement bind them into protons, neutrons and other hadrons. The four-minute format keeps the focus on the essentials.
takeaway: Quarks are the building blocks of matter, but confinement ensures they only appear in composite particles.

title: Neutron Stars, Pulsars, and Magnetars
coreQuestion: How do neutron stars become pulsars or magnetars, and what distinguishes them?
description: Launch Pad Astronomy compares pulsars and magnetars, explaining how a neutron star's magnetic field and rotation determine which form it takes.
takeaway: Pulsars and magnetars are the same kind of object distinguished by magnetic field strength and spin.

title: A Strange But Elegant Approach to a Surprisingly Hard Problem (GJK Algorithm)
coreQuestion: How can two convex shapes be tested for overlap without checking every point?
description: Reducible explains the Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi algorithm, which reduces collision detection to finding the origin inside a Minkowski difference. The video builds the idea from support functions. It reveals why the method is both elegant and fast.
takeaway: GJK turns overlap testing into a search for the origin inside a derived shape.

title: How Things Are Made | An Animated Introduction to Manufacturing Processes
coreQuestion: What are the main processes used to manufacture everyday objects?
description: Surveys casting, machining, forming and joining as routes from raw material to finished part. It provides an animated overview of production methods.
takeaway: Most products are shaped by a small set of fundamental manufacturing processes.

title: What is Natural Selection?
coreQuestion: How does differential survival shape traits across generations?
description: Breaks down natural selection into variation, inheritance and differential reproduction, using simple examples. It distinguishes selection from random change.
takeaway: Natural selection favours traits that improve reproductive success in a given environment, not strength or perfection.

title: This book should have changed mathematics forever
coreQuestion: Why can a book reshape a field in principle yet fail to change how mathematicians actually work?
description: Welch Labs looks at a historic mathematical text whose ideas were far ahead of their time, exploring its arguments and why its influence remained smaller than its author intended.
takeaway: A work's lasting impact depends as much on timing and accessibility as on the depth of its ideas.

title: The ULTRAVIOLET CATASTROPHE
coreQuestion: Why did classical physics predict an impossible infinite ultraviolet glow from hot objects?
description: The classical Rayleigh-Jeans law diverges at short wavelengths, and the video shows how Planck's quantisation of energy resolved the ultraviolet catastrophe. The result marks the birth of quantum theory.
takeaway: The ultraviolet catastrophe forced physics to abandon continuous energy and accept quantisation.

title: How James Webb's Instruments Work - and What They'll Show Us!
coreQuestion: What do Webb's instruments detect, and how do they turn light into science?
description: Launch Pad Astronomy describes Webb's instruments, from infrared detectors to spectrographs, and how they capture and analyse light from the early universe.
takeaway: Webb's power lies as much in its instruments as in its mirror, turning faint infrared light into data.

title: PageRank: A Trillion Dollar Algorithm
coreQuestion: How did PageRank turn the web's link structure into a search ranking?
description: Reducible derives PageRank from the idea of a random surfer, explaining how link counts become probabilities and how the stationary distribution ranks pages. The video connects the math to Google's early success. It notes the algorithm's limitations.
takeaway: PageRank ranks pages by the probability a random surfer lands on them.

title: The Problem with Titanium
coreQuestion: Why is titanium difficult to machine and weld despite its excellent properties?
description: Explains titanium's poor machinability and welding challenges arising from its strength and reactivity. It shows why high performance raises manufacturing cost.
takeaway: Titanium's outstanding properties come with manufacturing difficulties that raise cost and complexity.

title: Can Science Explain the Origin of Life?
coreQuestion: What scientific hypotheses address how life arose from non-living chemistry?
description: Reviews experimental and theoretical approaches to life's origins, including prebiotic synthesis, self-replicating molecules and compartmentalisation. It distinguishes open questions from established steps.
takeaway: The origin of life remains partly unsolved, but chemistry offers plausible pathways from simple molecules to self-replication.

title: What Integration Technique Should I Use? (trig sub, u sub, DI method, partial fractions) calculus 2
coreQuestion: How do you choose between u-substitution, trig substitution, partial fractions and integration by parts?
description: blackpenredpen works through representative integrals to show when each standard technique applies and how to recognise the right substitution or factorisation.
takeaway: Matching the structure of the integrand to the right technique is the key skill in integral calculus.

title: How does laser cooling work?
coreQuestion: How can light push atoms slow enough to reach temperatures near absolute zero?
description: By tuning lasers to exploit the Doppler effect, atoms absorb photons preferentially from the direction they move, losing momentum and cooling. The video connects this to trapping and ultracold experiments.
takeaway: Laser cooling uses photon momentum and frequency shifts to slow atoms, enabling ultracold physics.

title: Star Formation
coreQuestion: How do clouds of gas collapse to form new stars?
description: Launch Pad Astronomy follows star formation from cold molecular clouds through collapse and fragmentation to the ignition of nuclear fusion.
takeaway: Stars form when gravity overcomes pressure in cold clouds, triggering collapse and eventual fusion.

title: How are Microchips Made? 🖥️🛠️ CPU Manufacturing Process Steps
coreQuestion: How are microchips manufactured from silicon wafers?
description: Walks through wafer preparation, photolithography, doping and etching that build integrated circuits. It visualises the many steps behind a single chip.
takeaway: Microchips are built by repeatedly patterning and modifying silicon layers with extreme precision.

title: DNA vs RNA - Differences in Form and Function | Stated Clearly
coreQuestion: Why do cells use DNA for storage and RNA for messaging and catalysis?
description: Compares the structures and roles of DNA and RNA, focusing on sugar differences, stability and functional versatility. It explains why the division of labour matters for gene expression.
takeaway: DNA's stability suits long-term storage, while RNA's flexibility supports transient messages and catalytic roles.

title: Solving polynomial equations but they get increasingly awesome
coreQuestion: How do polynomial equations grow harder as their degree increases, and where do exact solutions break down?
description: blackpenredpen solves a sequence of polynomial equations of rising degree, illustrating the techniques that work for quadratics and cubics and the barriers that appear beyond.
takeaway: Exact algebraic solutions exist only up to degree four; beyond that, most polynomials resist closed-form roots.

title: Waves, Light and Sound - Physics 101 / AP Physics 1 Review with Dianna Cowern
coreQuestion: How do the shared properties of waves explain both light and sound phenomena?
description: A review of wave fundamentals, superposition, interference, diffraction and standing waves, applied to light and sound for introductory physics. The pace suits an AP-level refresher.
takeaway: Light and sound obey the same wave mathematics even though their physical mechanisms differ.

title: The Moon's Orbit and Eclipses
coreQuestion: Why do eclipses happen only sometimes, despite monthly new and full moons?
description: Launch Pad Astronomy explains why the Moon's tilted orbit means eclipses require alignment at the nodes, and how the Saros cycle predicts them.
takeaway: Eclipses are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted, so alignment with the Sun and Earth is infrequent.

title: How does Starlink Satellite Internet Work?📡☄🖥
coreQuestion: How does a constellation of low-Earth-orbit satellites deliver internet?
description: Explains Starlink's LEO satellites, phased-array antennas and ground stations that provide broadband. It shows how proximity reduces latency.
takeaway: LEO constellations reduce latency by bringing satellites closer, but require thousands of spacecraft.

title: Cell Biology | Cell Structure & Function
coreQuestion: How do organelles cooperate to keep a cell alive and functioning?
description: A lecture-style overview of cell structure and function, covering membranes, organelles, energy production and molecular transport. It builds a systems view of the cell.
takeaway: A cell is an integrated system whose organelles divide labour while depending on shared membranes and energy.

title: I want all trig functions in one integral!
coreQuestion: Can a single integral be constructed to contain every basic trigonometric function?
description: blackpenredpen builds an integral containing sine, cosine, tangent and their relatives, then works through the substitutions needed to evaluate it.
takeaway: Careful construction of an integrand can exercise several calculus techniques in one problem.

title: A better description of entropy
coreQuestion: What is a more accurate way to think about entropy than simple disorder?
description: Steve Mould refines the common disorder picture, explaining entropy as a count of microscopic configurations consistent with a macrostate. The argument is built from concrete examples rather than slogans.
takeaway: Entropy is about counting configurations, not about tidiness.

title: How massive stars die - with a BANG!
coreQuestion: What happens when a massive star reaches the end of its life?
description: Launch Pad Astronomy explains how massive stars burn through their fuel, collapse and explode as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes behind.
takeaway: A massive star's death is a supernova that forges heavy elements and leaves a compact remnant.

title: How does Computer Hardware Work? 💻🛠🔬 [3D Animated Teardown]
coreQuestion: What components make up a computer and how do they interact?
description: A 3D teardown of a computer showing the processor, memory, storage and buses that move data. It clarifies how hardware components cooperate.
takeaway: A computer's performance depends on how its processor, memory and buses exchange data.

title: Anatomy of the Brain | Model
coreQuestion: How are the brain's major regions organised and what do they do?
description: Uses a brain model to identify major structures and their functions, from the brainstem to the cortex and cerebellum. It provides a spatial framework for later neurobiology.
takeaway: Understanding brain anatomy starts with locating structures and linking them to broad functional roles.

title: solving equations but they get increasingly more impossible?
coreQuestion: What makes some equations solvable by hand while slightly altered versions become intractable?
description: blackpenredpen tackles an escalating series of equations, showing how small changes in form can push a problem from elementary algebra to numerical approximation.
takeaway: The boundary between solvable and unsolvable equations is often a matter of form rather than size.

title: Newton's Laws: Crash Course Physics #5
coreQuestion: How do Newton's three laws connect force, mass and acceleration?
description: CrashCourse introduces inertia, F=ma and action-reaction pairs, showing how they govern motion from projectiles to orbits. The episode works as a concise first pass over classical mechanics.
takeaway: Newton's laws reduce motion to the relationship between forces and changes in motion.

title: Unsettling Reasons The Universe May Be Beyond Understanding | Daniel Whiteson
coreQuestion: Are there fundamental limits to what humans can ever understand about the universe?
description: Daniel Whiteson discusses why some aspects of the universe may be permanently inaccessible, from horizons that hide information to the limits of our cognitive and instrumental reach.
takeaway: Science may face permanent boundaries set by physics itself, not just by our current technology.

title: How do Transistors Build into a CPU? 🖥️🤔 How do Transistors Work? 🖥️🤔
coreQuestion: How do billions of transistors combine to form a working CPU?
description: Shows how transistors form logic gates, then circuits, then a full processor on a single chip. It bridges device physics and computer architecture.
takeaway: Complex processors are built by hierarchically combining simple transistor switches.

title: Renal | Filtration, Reabsorption, and Secretion: Overview
coreQuestion: How do kidneys filter blood and reclaim useful substances?
description: Overview of renal physiology, explaining how the nephron filters plasma, reabsorbs nutrients and water, and secretes wastes. It connects structure to homeostasis.
takeaway: Kidney function is a selective pipeline: filter broadly, then reclaim what the body needs.

title: the last question on a Harvard-MIT Math Tournament!
coreQuestion: What kind of problem appears as the final question of a top-tier math competition?
description: blackpenredpen solves a problem from the Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament, explaining the insight that collapses an intimidating expression into a simple answer.
takeaway: Competition problems reward recognising hidden structure rather than brute-force computation.

title: Nuclear Chemistry: Crash Course Chemistry #38
coreQuestion: What happens inside an unstable nucleus, and how does that release energy?
description: The video covers radioactive decay, fission and the nuclear transformations that power reactors and weapons, with an introduction to half-lives. It bridges chemistry and nuclear physics for beginners.
takeaway: Nuclear reactions release energy by rearranging nucleons, not by breaking chemical bonds.

title: The Weirdest Stars in the Universe with Devesh Nandal
coreQuestion: What are the strangest types of stars known, and what physics produces them?
description: Devesh Nandal surveys unusual stellar objects, from extreme white dwarfs to exotic remnants, and the physics that creates them.
takeaway: The diversity of stars includes objects so extreme that they test the limits of known physics.

title: The $200M Machine that Prints Microchips: The EUV Photolithography System
coreQuestion: How does extreme ultraviolet lithography print features smaller than the light's wavelength?
description: Explains the EUV light source, reflective mirrors and resists that pattern nanometre-scale features. It shows how wavelength limits are overcome.
takeaway: EUV lithography overcomes wavelength limits using reflective optics and a plasma light source.

title: Renal | Kidney Anatomy Model
coreQuestion: What physical structures make up the kidney and urinary tract?
description: A model-based tour of kidney anatomy, identifying cortex, medulla, pyramids, calyces and the collecting system. It supports understanding of how urine is formed and transported.
takeaway: The kidney's layered anatomy reflects its stepwise processing of blood into urine.

title: i-th root of -1
coreQuestion: What does it mean to raise a number to the power of i, and what is the i-th root of -1?
description: blackpenredpen computes the i-th root of -1 using complex logarithms, illustrating how exponentiation becomes multi-valued in the complex plane.
takeaway: In the complex plane, roots and powers are multi-valued, so a single expression can yield infinitely many answers.

title: Magnetism: Crash Course Physics #32
coreQuestion: How do electric currents and magnetic fields relate to each other?
description: CrashCourse links moving charges, magnetic fields and induced currents, covering how electromagnets and generators work. The episode ties magnetism to electricity rather than treating them separately.
takeaway: Electricity and magnetism are two aspects of one electromagnetic interaction.

title: How We Are Going to the Moon - 4K
coreQuestion: What is the plan for returning humans to the Moon under the Artemis programme?
description: NASA outlines the Artemis missions, the rockets, spacecraft and lunar orbit infrastructure intended to return astronauts to the Moon and prepare for Mars.
takeaway: The Artemis programme is designed as a sustained return to the Moon rather than a single visit.

title: HOW ROCKETS ARE MADE (Rocket Factory Tour - United Launch Alliance) - Smarter Every Day 231
coreQuestion: How are large launch vehicles assembled from raw materials into flight-ready hardware?
description: A walkthrough of United Launch Alliance's factory, following the fabrication and integration of a rocket from tank welding through engine installation and final assembly. It shows how precision manufacturing and testing at each stage feed into a flight-ready vehicle.
takeaway: Building a rocket is a sequence of precision manufacturing steps where each subsystem is integrated and tested before flight.

title: Immunology | Immune System: Overview
coreQuestion: How do innate and adaptive defences coordinate to protect the body?
description: Overview of immune defence, from barriers and phagocytes to antigen-specific lymphocytes and memory. It frames immunity as a coordinated, layered response.
takeaway: Effective immunity depends on rapid first responders and precise, memory-capable adaptive cells working together.

title: Oxford MAT asks: sin(72 degrees)
coreQuestion: How can sin 72 degrees be expressed exactly using radicals?
description: blackpenredpen derives the exact value of sin 72 degrees, connecting the angle to the golden ratio and a nested radical expression.
takeaway: Special angles like 72 degrees hide simple radical values that emerge from the geometry of the pentagon.

title: Quantum Mechanics - Part 1: Crash Course Physics #43
coreQuestion: What makes quantum mechanics fundamentally different from classical physics?
description: CrashCourse introduces wave-particle duality, quantisation and uncertainty as the core departures from classical intuition. The episode is pitched as a first encounter with quantum ideas.
takeaway: Quantum mechanics replaces definite trajectories with probabilities governed by wavefunctions.

title: Cosmic Dawn (NASA+ Original Documentary)
coreQuestion: What did the James Webb Space Telescope reveal about the universe's first stars and galaxies?
description: A NASA+ documentary following the James Webb Space Telescope's first deep observations of the early universe, from the formation of the first stars to the emergence of galaxies.
takeaway: JWST's infrared vision pushes the observable frontier back to the era when the first light filled the cosmos.

title: 1: Introduction to Neural Networks and Deep Learning; Training Deep NNs
coreQuestion: How do neural networks learn, and what makes deep training difficult?
description: MIT's lecture introduces neural networks and the training of deep models, covering forward passes, loss and gradient-based updates. The video discusses depth, representation and optimisation challenges. It bridges theory and practice.
takeaway: Deep learning trains layered representations by propagating errors backward through the network.

title: How Engines Work - (See Through Engine in Slow Motion) - Smarter Every Day 166
coreQuestion: How does a four-stroke internal combustion engine convert fuel into motion?
description: Slow-motion footage through a transparent engine reveals intake, compression, combustion and exhaust as the piston and crankshaft transform pressure into rotating power. The visualization links each mechanical motion to the underlying thermodynamic cycle.
takeaway: An engine is a controlled explosion timed to push a piston, whose motion is converted to continuous rotation by the crankshaft.

title: Bacteria | Structure and Function
coreQuestion: How does bacterial cell structure support survival and reproduction?
description: Long-form bacterial biology covering cell walls, membranes, motility, genetics and reproduction. It explains how structural features enable diverse lifestyles.
takeaway: Bacteria's simple but adaptable architecture underlies their ubiquity and resilience.

title: Necessity of complex numbers
coreQuestion: Why are complex numbers unavoidable once we try to solve polynomial equations?
description: MIT OpenCourseWare motivates the complex numbers by showing how quadratic equations with no real roots force an extension of the number system.
takeaway: Complex numbers are not an invention but a completion: they make every nonconstant polynomial solvable.

title: Traveling Waves: Crash Course Physics #17
coreQuestion: What determines how fast a wave travels through a medium?
description: The video derives wave speed from frequency and wavelength, and shows how transverse and longitudinal waves propagate. The relationship is presented with worked examples.
takeaway: A wave's speed is set by the medium, while frequency and wavelength trade off to match it.

title: What Is an Exoplanet?
coreQuestion: What counts as an exoplanet, and how do astronomers find worlds beyond our solar system?
description: A short NASA explainer defining exoplanets and outlining the main detection techniques, from transit dips to stellar wobbles.
takeaway: Most exoplanets are found indirectly, by measuring how they alter their host star's light or motion.

title: I Explored the World's First Nuclear Power Plant (and How It Works) - Smarter Every Day 306
coreQuestion: How does the world's first nuclear power plant generate electricity from fission?
description: A tour of a pioneering reactor shows how uranium fission releases heat, coolant carries it to a steam turbine, and control rods regulate the chain reaction. The visit connects the plant's history to the basic physics of nuclear power.
takeaway: Nuclear power plants turn the heat of fission into steam-driven electricity while control rods keep the reaction steady.

title: Why Cancer is So Hard to Kill
coreQuestion: Why do cancers resist treatment and recur after therapy?
description: Explains cancer as uncontrolled growth compounded by genetic diversity, metastasis and resistance to therapy. It uses anatomy and pathology to show why elimination is difficult.
takeaway: Cancer is hard to cure because tumours evolve, spread and exploit the body's own systems.

title: 1. Probability Models and Axioms
coreQuestion: What are the axioms that make probability a consistent mathematical theory?
description: MIT OpenCourseWare introduces probability as a model built on sample spaces, events and three axioms, laying the groundwork for all later theorems.
takeaway: Probability rests on a small set of axioms that turn uncertainty into measurable, consistent mathematics.

title: Entropy: Embrace the Chaos! Crash Course Chemistry #20
coreQuestion: Why do some reactions proceed on their own while others need a push?
description: Entropy is tied to spontaneity and Gibbs free energy, showing how disorder and enthalpy together determine reaction direction. The chemistry framing keeps the thermodynamics concrete.
takeaway: Spontaneity depends on both energy change and the increase in entropy.

title: 50 Years of Mars Exploration
coreQuestion: How has robotic exploration of Mars evolved over five decades?
description: A NASA JPL retrospective tracing missions from early flybys to modern rovers, and the engineering challenges of operating on Mars.
takeaway: Each Mars mission builds on the last, turning a distant planet into an increasingly familiar landscape.

title: This TRANSPARENT ENGINE is Fascinating (How Engines Work) - Smarter Every Day 292
coreQuestion: What happens inside a running engine that you can only see through a transparent block?
description: A see-through engine lets you watch valves open, fuel ignite and pistons cycle in real time, linking each mechanical motion to the four-stroke thermodynamic cycle. The footage makes timing and coordination visible rather than abstract.
takeaway: Seeing the cycle in motion makes clear that timing, not just force, is what makes an engine run smoothly.

title: Why Even Fit People Are At Risk of a Heart Attack
coreQuestion: How can atherosclerosis threaten people who appear healthy and fit?
description: Examines how plaque builds in arteries, why rupture can cause sudden heart attacks and why fitness does not eliminate risk. It connects anatomy with prevention.
takeaway: Heart attack risk depends on arterial plaque and inflammation, not just outward fitness.

title: The Big Picture of Linear Algebra
coreQuestion: How do the four fundamental subspaces organise everything in linear algebra?
description: MIT OpenCourseWare steps back to show how matrices, vector spaces and the four fundamental subspaces fit together into one coherent picture.
takeaway: Linear algebra is less about formulas and more about the geometry of spaces and the maps between them.

title: Thermodynamics: Crash Course Physics #23
coreQuestion: How do the laws of thermodynamics constrain what engines and refrigerators can do?
description: CrashCourse walks through the first and second laws, relating heat, work and efficiency limits for thermal machines. The episode connects abstract principles to engines and refrigerators.
takeaway: No heat engine can be perfectly efficient; some energy is always lost to entropy.

title: The Insane Engineering of James Webb Telescope
coreQuestion: What engineering problems had to be solved to fold a 6.5-metre telescope into a rocket fairing?
description: Real Engineering examines the James Webb Space Telescope's folded architecture, from its segmented gold mirrors to the multi-layer sunshield that keeps its instruments cold.
takeaway: JWST's design is a sequence of controlled transformations, each of which had to work perfectly in space.

title: INSIDE a Nuclear Reactor Core - Smarter Every Day 317
coreQuestion: What does the inside of a nuclear reactor core look like and how does it stay safe?
description: Footage from inside an operating reactor core shows fuel assemblies, control mechanisms and shielding, explaining how fission heat is managed and contained. The tour emphasizes geometry and materials that keep the reaction controlled.
takeaway: A reactor core is a carefully shielded arrangement where geometry and materials keep fission controlled and heat recoverable.

title: The REAL Reason Diabetes Is So Dangerous
coreQuestion: What makes diabetes dangerous beyond high blood sugar itself?
description: Explains diabetes as a systemic disorder affecting vessels, nerves and organs, not merely elevated glucose. It clarifies acute and chronic complications.
takeaway: Diabetes is dangerous because prolonged high glucose damages blood vessels and organs throughout the body.

title: Overview of Differential Equations
coreQuestion: What are the main types of differential equations, and what does solving one mean?
description: MIT OpenCourseWare surveys ordinary differential equations, their classifications and the idea that a solution is a function satisfying a rate-of-change relation.
takeaway: A differential equation describes how a quantity changes, and solving it means finding the function that obeys that rule.

title: Why Does Everything Decay Into Lead
coreQuestion: Why does radioactive decay so often end in lead?
description: The video traces decay chains down the periodic table, explaining how successive emissions drive heavy nuclei toward stable lead isotopes. The endpoint reflects nuclear stability rather than coincidence.
takeaway: Lead is a common endpoint because its nucleus is especially stable among heavy elements.

title: Loop Quantum Gravity Explained
coreQuestion: Can space itself be quantised into discrete loops, and does that resolve singularities?
description: PBS Space Time introduces loop quantum gravity, which treats spacetime as a network of quantised loops and aims to remove the infinities of classical general relativity.
takeaway: Loop quantum gravity replaces smooth spacetime with a discrete structure, but its predictions remain experimentally untested.

title: Boolean Logic & Logic Gates: Crash Course Computer Science #3
coreQuestion: How do logic gates build the foundation of all digital circuits?
description: CrashCourse explains Boolean logic and how AND, OR and NOT gates compose into larger circuits. The video shows truth tables and simple combinations. It connects logic to physical hardware.
takeaway: All digital computation reduces to combinations of simple true-or-false operations.

title: Making YBCO superconductor
coreQuestion: How is a YBCO high-temperature superconductor fabricated from raw powders?
description: The video demonstrates mixing, pressing and sintering yttrium barium copper oxide, then cooling it with liquid nitrogen to demonstrate zero resistance. It shows how composition and heat treatment determine superconducting behavior.
takeaway: Superconductivity emerges from precise composition and heat treatment, not from the material alone.

title: Why Pancreatic Cancer is So Deadly
coreQuestion: What features make pancreatic cancer especially lethal?
description: Reviews why pancreatic cancer is often detected late, grows aggressively and resists treatment. It links anatomy, symptoms and disease progression.
takeaway: Pancreatic cancer's late detection and rapid spread make it one of the deadliest malignancies.

title: Lecture 1: Sets, Set Operations and Mathematical Induction
coreQuestion: How do sets, their operations and mathematical induction form the language of mathematics?
description: MIT OpenCourseWare's first discrete-mathematics lecture covers sets, unions, intersections, complements and the principle of mathematical induction.
takeaway: Induction turns a base case and a step into a proof for infinitely many statements at once.

title: So what IS the Higgs boson?
coreQuestion: How does the Higgs field give mass to some particles but not others?
description: SciShow explains the Higgs mechanism, in which particles acquire mass by interacting with a field that permeates space. The boson itself is a ripple of that field, not the source of mass directly.
takeaway: Mass arises from interaction with the Higgs field, not from the Higgs boson itself.

title: How The Space Shuttle Lost Its Jet Engines
coreQuestion: Why did the Space Shuttle abandon jet engines for landing and rely on gliding instead?
description: Scott Manley explains the design history behind the Shuttle's landing approach, including why air-breathing engines were dropped in favour of an unpowered glide.
takeaway: Engineering decisions often trade capability for mass, reliability and mission simplicity.

title: Registers and RAM: Crash Course Computer Science #6
coreQuestion: How do registers and RAM store and provide data to the processor?
description: CrashCourse covers registers and RAM, explaining how the CPU holds immediate values and how main memory supplies larger working data. The video introduces the memory hierarchy. It shows the speed gap between the two.
takeaway: Registers are the CPU's fastest scratch space; RAM holds the working set at a distance.

title: Welding visualization system uses intense pulsed lighting to outshine electric arc, laser cutter
coreQuestion: How can a camera see through the blinding glare of an electric welding arc?
description: A high-speed imaging system uses intense pulsed lighting to outshine the arc, revealing droplet transfer and pool dynamics during welding. The technique turns an opaque glare into observable metal transfer.
takeaway: Overpowering the arc's light with timed pulses turns an opaque glare into observable metal transfer.

title: Why Sciatica is So Hard To Fix
coreQuestion: Why is sciatic nerve pain so persistent and difficult to treat?
description: Explains sciatica as irritation or compression of the sciatic nerve, often from spinal issues, and why symptoms can linger. It distinguishes causes and management limits.
takeaway: Sciatic pain is hard to fix because the underlying nerve compression can have multiple, stubborn causes.

title: Aristotle's Wheel Paradox - To Infinity and Beyond
coreQuestion: How can two wheels of different radii travel the same distance in one rotation without slipping?
description: Up and Atom unpacks the classical paradox of Aristotle's wheel, showing why the apparent contradiction comes from misapplying the no-slip condition.
takeaway: The paradox dissolves once you track which points actually touch the ground and how they move.

title: Our Universe Shouldn't Exist | The Matter-Antimatter Problem
coreQuestion: If matter and antimatter were created equally, why is the universe made of matter?
description: The video examines the matter-antimatter imbalance and the small asymmetries that may have let matter survive annihilation. The question remains open but the candidate mechanisms are surveyed.
takeaway: A tiny excess of matter over antimatter in the early universe is why anything exists today.

title: A Galaxy with NO STARS - Deep Sky Videos
coreQuestion: How can a galaxy contain almost no stars yet still be considered a galaxy?
description: Deep Sky Videos discusses a galaxy whose mass is dominated by dark matter, with so few stars that it challenges conventional pictures of galaxy formation.
takeaway: Galaxies are defined by their mass and structure, not merely by their visible stars.

title: Representing Numbers and Letters with Binary: Crash Course Computer Science #4
coreQuestion: How do binary digits represent numbers and letters in a computer?
description: CrashCourse explains binary representation of numbers and text, covering place value, signed integers and character encodings. The video shows how bits become meaningful symbols. It underpins later hardware topics.
takeaway: All data in a computer is ultimately a pattern of bits given meaning by convention.

title: DIY mass spectrometer measures potassium in dietary salt substitute
coreQuestion: How can a homemade mass spectrometer identify and quantify potassium in a salt substitute?
description: A do-it-yourself spectrometer ionizes a sample and measures flight times to separate ions by mass, revealing the potassium content of a dietary substitute. It demonstrates how mass-based identification works even with modest hardware.
takeaway: Mass spectrometry identifies substances by the masses of their ions, even with modest homemade hardware.

title: What Really Happens to Dead Bodies That Are Donated to Science
coreQuestion: How are donated bodies used in medical education and research?
description: Describes the handling, preservation and educational use of donated bodies, and how they support anatomy training. It addresses ethics and process without sensationalism.
takeaway: Body donation provides an irreplaceable foundation for training clinicians and advancing anatomical knowledge.

title: The 379 page proof that 1+1=2
coreQuestion: Why did proving 1+1=2 require hundreds of pages in Principia Mathematica?
description: Up and Atom traces how Russell and Whitehead built arithmetic from pure logic, showing why even the simplest truth needed an enormous formal scaffolding.
takeaway: The length of the proof reflects the ambition of deriving all mathematics from logic, not the difficulty of the fact itself.

title: Quarks: The Miracle That Saved Particle Physics
coreQuestion: How did the quark model bring order to the chaotic zoo of hadrons?
description: SciShow recounts how quarks organised dozens of apparently unrelated particles into a simple scheme based on a few fundamental constituents. The model turned a confusing catalogue into a predictive framework.
takeaway: Quarks reduced a bewildering particle zoo to combinations of a handful of fundamental building blocks.

title: What Earth’s Final Biosphere Will Look Like | Jacob Haqq Misra
coreQuestion: What will Earth's last habitable environment look like as the Sun brightens over billions of years?
description: Event Horizon hosts a long-form talk on the far future of Earth's biosphere, tracing how rising solar luminosity will shrink habitable zones and reshape life.
takeaway: Earth's biosphere has an expiry date set by the Sun, but the timeline stretches across billions of years.

title: Keyboard interface hardware
coreQuestion: How does a keyboard send keystrokes to a computer at the hardware level?
description: Ben Eater builds and explains the hardware interface between a keyboard and a microprocessor, covering scanning, encoding and serial transmission.
takeaway: A keystroke becomes data through a chain of electrical signals, encoding and protocol timing.

title: Details in the process of making "blacker than vantablack" coatings (part 1?)
coreQuestion: What manufacturing details make a coating darker than Vantablack?
description: The video examines deposition and handling steps that produce an ultra-black coating, focusing on how nanostructured surfaces trap nearly all incident light. It highlights process control rather than pigment chemistry.
takeaway: Extreme blackness comes from nanostructure that traps light through multiple absorption, not from pigment alone.

title: Is Your Liver in Danger? Understanding Fatty Liver Disease
coreQuestion: How does fat accumulation damage the liver and what can reverse it?
description: Explains non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, its progression from fat buildup to inflammation and fibrosis, and lifestyle factors that influence risk. It emphasises early detection.
takeaway: Fatty liver disease can progress silently, but early metabolic changes are often reversible.

title: The Oldest Unsolved Problem in Math
coreQuestion: Why has a centuries-old conjecture about primes resisted proof despite its simple statement?
description: Veritasium explores a centuries-old conjecture about prime numbers, explaining why its simplicity hides deep difficulty.
takeaway: A problem can be easy to state yet require mathematics that does not yet exist to solve.

title: 20. How Nuclear Energy Works
coreQuestion: How is the energy released by nuclear fission captured and controlled in a reactor?
description: An MIT lecture covers fission, neutron moderation and reactor design, showing how a self-sustaining chain reaction is regulated for power generation. The treatment is aimed at undergraduates.
takeaway: Nuclear power harnesses controlled fission, using moderators and control rods to keep the chain reaction steady.

title: Where Do Stars Come From? 4K
coreQuestion: How do clouds of gas and dust collapse to ignite nuclear fusion and form stars?
description: Astrum walks through the stages of star formation, from giant molecular clouds to protostars and the ignition of fusion.
takeaway: Stars are born when gravity overcomes pressure in cold gas clouds, compressing matter until fusion begins.

title: Let's build a digital clock!
coreQuestion: How can basic logic chips be wired together to keep and display time?
description: Ben Eater assembles a digital clock from discrete logic components, explaining counters, dividers and display drivers along the way.
takeaway: Complex digital devices can be built from simple, well-understood logic blocks.

title: Drawing electricity from this sodium-water reactor prevents it from exploding (in theory)
coreQuestion: How can extracting electricity from a sodium-water reaction keep the reactor from exploding?
description: The video explores a sodium-water reactor design where drawing off electrical energy limits the reaction's thermal runaway, at least in theory. It examines how energy removal can act as a stabilizing feedback.
takeaway: Removing energy from a reactive system as electricity can act as a stabilizing feedback that prevents runaway heating.

title: The Insane Biology of: The Octopus
coreQuestion: What makes the octopus nervous system and body plan so different from other animals?
description: Real Science examines the octopus's distributed brain, colour-changing skin and problem-solving behaviour.
takeaway: An octopus thinks with both its central brain and its arms, a radically different organisation from vertebrates.

title: The line that broke mathematicians for 2000 years
coreQuestion: Why did Euclid's parallel postulate trouble mathematicians for two millennia?
description: Veritasium tells the story of the parallel postulate and how its eventual abandonment created non-Euclidean geometries.
takeaway: Questioning a single axiom can open entirely new mathematical worlds.

title: Laser Fundamentals I | MIT Understanding Lasers and Fiberoptics
coreQuestion: What physical conditions must be met to produce coherent laser light?
description: An MIT course lecture derives stimulated emission, population inversion and cavity feedback, explaining how lasers achieve coherence. The derivation is more formal than a typical explainer.
takeaway: Laser action requires population inversion and an optical cavity to amplify coherent light.

title: Could Neptune’s Moon Triton Be Habitable?
coreQuestion: Could Neptune's moon Triton harbour conditions suitable for life beneath its icy surface?
description: Astrum examines Triton's geology, its thin atmosphere and the possibility of a subsurface ocean that might support microbial life.
takeaway: Even distant, frozen moons can harbour internal heat and liquid water, expanding where life might exist.

title: 12. Greedy Algorithms: Minimum Spanning Tree
coreQuestion: Why do greedy algorithms produce minimum spanning trees, and when do they fail?
description: MIT OpenCourseWare's lecture on greedy algorithms proves why locally optimal choices yield a globally minimum spanning tree and examines the conditions required.
takeaway: Greedy methods work when a problem has optimal substructure and the greedy choice property.

title: 3D-printed, alcohol-powered, Einstein-Szilard absorption refrigerator
coreQuestion: How can a refrigerator run on heat and alcohol instead of a compressor?
description: A 3D-printed Einstein-Szilard absorption refrigerator uses heat and an alcohol working fluid to drive cooling without moving parts. The build demonstrates heat-driven refrigeration in a compact form.
takeaway: Absorption refrigeration converts thermal energy into cooling, trading efficiency for mechanical simplicity and quiet operation.

title: A Journey Across Africa | BBC Earth
coreQuestion: How do diverse African ecosystems shape the behaviour and survival of their wildlife?
description: BBC Earth presents a sweeping journey across African habitats, linking landscape, climate and the animals that inhabit them.
takeaway: Africa's varied environments drive equally varied strategies for survival among its wildlife.

title: The Discovery That Transformed Pi
coreQuestion: What discovery changed how mathematicians compute and understand pi?
description: Veritasium traces the history of pi computation, highlighting the breakthrough that transformed it from a geometric ratio into a computable constant.
takeaway: Pi's value became accessible through infinite series, turning an impossible measurement into arithmetic.

title: Special Relativity: Crash Course Physics #42
coreQuestion: What happens to space and time when objects move near the speed of light?
description: CrashCourse introduces special relativity, covering inertial frames, time dilation and length contraction.
takeaway: Space and time are not absolute but depend on the observer's motion.

title: The Alchemy of Neutron Star Collisions
coreQuestion: How do neutron star collisions create heavy elements like gold?
description: PBS Space Time explains how merging neutron stars forge heavy elements through rapid neutron capture and broadcast gravitational waves.
takeaway: The heaviest elements in the universe are forged in the collision of dead stars.

title: Why My Teenage Code Was Terrible: Sorting Algorithms and Big O Notation
coreQuestion: Why does a naive sorting algorithm become painfully slow as input size grows?
description: Tom Scott revisits his early code to show how bubble sort's quadratic growth makes it impractical, introducing Big O notation as a way to compare algorithms.
takeaway: An algorithm's growth rate matters more than its speed on small inputs.

title: The Ridiculous Engineering Of Jet Engines
coreQuestion: How do jet engines compress, combust and expand air to produce thrust?
description: Veritasium details the engineering of jet engines, from intake and compression through combustion and turbine-driven expansion.
takeaway: A jet engine is a continuous thermodynamic cycle that converts fuel energy into directed thrust.

title: 10 Animal Behaviours Filmed for the First Time Ever | BBC Earth
coreQuestion: Which animal behaviours were captured on film for the first time, and what do they reveal?
description: BBC Earth compiles ten behaviours never previously filmed, explaining the observations and methods behind each discovery.
takeaway: New filming technology continues to reveal behaviours that reshape our understanding of animal life.

title: The Banach–Tarski Paradox
coreQuestion: How can a solid sphere be decomposed and reassembled into two identical copies?
description: Vsauce explains the Banach-Tarski paradox, where a sphere is cut into pieces and reassembled into two copies using the axiom of choice.
takeaway: The paradox is a consequence of non-measurable sets and the axiom of choice, not a physical operation.

title: Why is there antimatter?
coreQuestion: Why does the universe contain matter rather than equal parts matter and antimatter?
description: Veritasium examines the imbalance between matter and antimatter, exploring CP violation and the conditions of the early universe.
takeaway: A small asymmetry in the early universe left matter dominant, enabling everything we see.

title: What Does Dark Energy Really Do?
coreQuestion: What does dark energy do to the expansion of the universe?
description: PBS Space Time examines dark energy's role in accelerating cosmic expansion and the evidence behind it.
takeaway: Dark energy drives the accelerating expansion of the universe, though its nature remains unknown.

title: How Binary Search Makes Computers Much, Much Faster
coreQuestion: How does halving the search space each step make binary search exponentially faster than linear search?
description: Tom Scott explains how repeatedly halving an ordered list turns a linear scan into a logarithmic search.
takeaway: Binary search trades the requirement of sorted data for exponentially fewer comparisons.

title: I got buried in concrete to explain how it works
coreQuestion: How does concrete cure and harden, and what happens to objects trapped inside it?
description: Veritasium is buried in concrete to demonstrate how the material sets, releases heat and develops strength over time.
takeaway: Concrete hardens through chemical hydration, not drying, and its strength grows for weeks after pouring.

title: Microbiology - Viruses (Structure, Types and Bacteriophage Replication)
coreQuestion: How are viruses structured, and how do bacteriophages replicate inside bacteria?
description: Armando Hasudungan reviews virus morphology and the replication cycle of bacteriophages within bacterial hosts.
takeaway: Viruses are obligate parasites that hijack host machinery to replicate their genetic material.

title: How To Count Past Infinity
coreQuestion: How can there be different sizes of infinity, and what lies beyond countable infinity?
description: Vsauce explores Cantor's discovery that infinities come in different sizes and how counting can extend beyond the infinite.
takeaway: Infinity is not a single quantity; Cantor showed there are infinitely many sizes of infinity.

title: How do Superconductors work at the Quantum level?
coreQuestion: How do superconductors conduct electricity without resistance at the quantum level?
description: Arvin Ash explains superconductivity through Cooper pairs and the BCS theory that accounts for zero resistance.
takeaway: Superconductivity arises when electrons pair up and move collectively without scattering.

title: The Real Largest Star
coreQuestion: Which star is actually the largest known, and how do we measure stellar sizes?
description: SEA investigates the largest known stars, discussing measurement challenges and the physical limits of stellar size.
takeaway: The largest stars are rare, unstable red supergiants whose sizes push the limits of stellar physics.

title: The Perfect Battery Material Is Dangerous
coreQuestion: Why is lithium the ideal battery material despite its reactivity and safety risks?
description: Veritasium explores why lithium's electrochemical properties make it unmatched for batteries, and why that same reactivity creates fire hazards.
takeaway: The properties that make lithium an excellent battery material also make it dangerous to mishandle.

title: 23. Stem Cells
coreQuestion: What distinguishes stem cells, and how do they differentiate into specialised tissues?
description: MIT OpenCourseWare's lecture on stem cells covers their defining properties, differentiation pathways and therapeutic potential.
takeaway: Stem cells combine self-renewal with the capacity to become specialised cell types.

title: Integration and the fundamental theorem of calculus | Chapter 8, Essence of calculus
coreQuestion: Why does the fundamental theorem of calculus connect differentiation and integration?
description: 3Blue1Brown visualises how summing infinitely thin rectangles leads to antiderivatives, unifying two seemingly separate operations.
takeaway: Differentiation and integration are inverse processes, linked by the fundamental theorem.

title: How Does a Transistor Work?
coreQuestion: How does a transistor use a small signal to control a larger current?
description: Veritasium explains the transistor as a semiconductor device whose gate controls current flow, enabling amplification and switching.
takeaway: A transistor is a voltage-controlled switch and amplifier built from doped semiconductor junctions.

title: Genetic Engineering
coreQuestion: How do scientists directly modify an organism's DNA to change its traits?
description: Amoeba Sisters introduces genetic engineering, explaining how DNA is cut, inserted and expressed to alter organisms.
takeaway: Genetic engineering gives precise control over traits by rewriting the instructions in DNA.

title: The Nucleus: Crash Course Chemistry #1
coreQuestion: What is an atomic nucleus made of, and what holds it together?
description: Hank Green tours the atomic nucleus: protons, neutrons and the strong nuclear force that overcomes electrostatic repulsion to bind the nucleus together, plus a look at isotopes and radioactive decay.
takeaway: The nucleus is a dense core of protons and neutrons held together by the strong nuclear force, far stronger than electromagnetism at short range.

title: Making purple gold
coreQuestion: Can gold and aluminium be combined into a purple intermetallic alloy?
description: NileRed attempts to make purple gold, an intermetallic compound of gold and aluminium, walking through alloy formation, oxidation and careful temperature control.
takeaway: Purple gold is a real intermetallic alloy, but it is brittle and tricky to make without the right stoichiometry and conditions.

title: The Professor's Top 10 - Periodic Table of Videos
coreQuestion: Which elements does a career chemist rate as the most remarkable?
description: Martyn Poliakoff picks ten favourite elements from the periodic table and explains what makes each one chemically distinctive after a career in chemistry.
takeaway: The periodic table is full of elements with unique personalities, from explosively reactive metals to dense, stubborn transition metals.

title: How Air Conditioning Works
coreQuestion: How does an air conditioner move heat from indoors to outdoors using refrigerant chemistry?
description: The American Chemical Society's Reactions series explains how air conditioners use evaporating and condensing refrigerant to move heat against the temperature gradient.
takeaway: Air conditioners don't create cold; they move heat from inside a building to the outside using a refrigerant that cycles between liquid and gas.

title: The Evolution of Scorpions
coreQuestion: How did an ancient marine arthropod become one of the most successful land predators?
description: A palaeontological tour of scorpion ancestry, from Silurian sea scorpions to the armoured, venomous land predators that survive today, and the adaptations that let them exploit deserts.
takeaway: Scorpions are a rare case of an ancient body plan staying competitive for hundreds of millions of years with modest changes.

title: Why Did Mammals Survive When Dinosaurs Didn't?
coreQuestion: What did mammals have that let them inherit the Earth after the asteroid?
description: A feature-length look at the extinction that ended the dinosaurs and the small, warm-blooded animals that came through it, tracing how body size, diet and reproduction shaped who survived.
takeaway: Surviving a mass extinction is less about being powerful than about being able to wait out a collapsed food web.

title: The Insane Biology of: The Greenland Shark
coreQuestion: How does a shark survive for four centuries in near-freezing darkness?
description: An examination of the Greenland shark's extraordinary lifespan, slow metabolism and parasite-loaded eyes, and what its biology implies about ageing in cold-water vertebrates.
